title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model can improve middle school students’ math learning, particularly for students from low-income backgrounds and for lower-performing subgroups. The authors are motivated by persistent access and engagement gaps in mathematics tutoring, and they ask whether combining adaptive math software with human tutoring can increase students’ learning opportunities and whether effects differ by baseline ability.

The intervention is a hybrid tutoring approach in which students work with AI-based math software while human tutors provide motivational, relational, and content support. Across three quasi-experimental studies, the model was implemented during the school day in three urban U.S. middle schools using different software platforms: IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia. Two sites used a round-robin tutoring structure without a dashboard, while the third piloted a tutor-facing dashboard intended to guide support. The sites included largely low-income student populations, including a Pennsylvania middle school, a large California middle school, and a small Pennsylvania charter school serving Black male students.

The findings indicate that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased engagement and intermediate learning outcomes such as time on task, questions answered, skills proficient, lesson completion, and workspace progress. The strongest pattern was that lower-pretest or below-grade-level students benefited more than higher-performing students. The authors conclude that hybrid tutoring can improve learning opportunities at relatively low marginal cost, and that dashboard-guided support and more targeted tutor allocation may further increase equity and effectiveness.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental, multi-site field study with mixed-effects models and interrupted time series analyses, but it lacks random assignment and has site-specific implementation differences. The design provides reasonably strong causal evidence, though internal validity concerns keep it below blue.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows modest-to-meaningful positive effects on key engagement and progress measures in a priority population of low-income middle school students, including a statistically significant tutoring effect and evidence of stronger benefits for lower-pretest students. The reported effects are promising but are mostly intermediate outcomes rather than external achievement test gains, so overall impact is best classified as green.

interventions.use_case: hybrid human-AI tutoring in middle school math, where students work in software such as IXL, i-Ready, or MATHia while remote human tutors provide motivational, relationship-building, and occasional content support; in one site tutors were guided by a live dashboard

finding.finding_summary: This three-study quasi-experimental investigation found that hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software alone. In Site 1, adding a math teacher and then tutoring increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient; the mixed-effects model showed a positive tutoring effect on time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006) over n=125 students, with similar positive effects for questions answered and skills proficient. In Site 2, tutoring increased lessons passed per week (β=0.244, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381], p<0.001; n=385), and in Site 3 students completed 0.36 more MATHia workspaces per hour after tutor-to-student ratios improved from 1:8 to 1:4 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], p=.03; n=75).
finding.measure: Math software usage and progress: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed per week, and MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also improved engagement with learning software, a proximate social-emotional/behavioral outcome emphasized throughout the paper. Across sites, students spent more time on task during hybrid tutoring than with software alone (e.g., Site 2 increased from 24 to 33 minutes per week), suggesting greater persistence and participation. The authors interpret these gains as especially strong for lower-pretest students, who appear to respond more to tutor support and relationship-building.
finding.measure: Time on task / minutes spent using math software; participation and engagement indicators
finding.effect_size: β=0.202 on time spent; observed increase from 24 to 33 minutes/week
finding.confidence_interval: [0.057, 0.347] for tutoring effect on time spent; other site-level intervals reported in text

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the hybrid model can improve tutoring efficiency and scalability by allowing one tutor to serve more students and by using dashboard guidance to allocate attention. The discussion emphasizes a lower marginal cost of about $700 per student annually, substantially below traditional high-dosage tutoring costs of $3,500-$4,300, while still producing positive engagement and progress outcomes.
finding.measure: Marginal cost per student; tutor-to-student ratio; time per tutor session
